say.en: The third family of data-parallel machines is the one in every gaming laptop and every AI data centre: the GPU. This video introduces how it is programmed, with CUDA, and the hierarchy of threads, blocks and grids.
Here are the eight stages.
Where GPUs came from, the host and device model, DAXPY in CUDA, and threads, blocks and grids.
Then how a thread finds its element, two-dimensional grids, CUDA in vector terms, and an exam question.
Stage 1: GPUs were built for graphics. A screen has millions of pixels, and each is computed in the same way.
That is data-level parallelism on an enormous scale.
In 2007 NVIDIA released CUDA, an extension of C that lets programmers use the GPU for any computation, not just graphics.
OpenCL is an open standard built on the same model. We use CUDA, as the textbook does.
Stage 2: a GPU does not run on its own. The host is the CPU, running the ordinary program.
The device is the GPU, with its own memory. Data must be in GPU memory before the GPU can use it.
The host calls kernels: functions that the device runs with thousands of threads at once.
In the code, a kernel is marked double underscore global: called from the host, run on the device. This is heterogeneous computing: two kinds of processor, each doing what it does best.

say.en: Stage 3: DAXPY in CUDA. The kernel is written for one element.
Each thread first works out which element it owns, from its block number and its thread number within the block.
Then, if that element exists, it does one multiply-add. There is no loop at all: the loop has become the threads.
The host launches the kernel with triple angle brackets: the number of blocks, then the threads per block. 256 threads per block, and enough blocks to cover n.

do.text: write the code for one element

say.en: Stage 4: the hierarchy. A thread is one instance of the kernel, usually handling one element. The textbook's example has 8192 elements, so 8192 threads.
Threads are grouped into thread blocks. A block runs on one streaming multiprocessor, an SM, and its threads can cooperate. Here, 512 threads per block.
All the blocks of one launch form the grid: 8192 over 512, 16 blocks.
Every thread can read built-in variables: its threadIdx and blockIdx, and the sizes blockDim and gridDim.
Within a block, threads share fast on-chip memory, and can wait for each other at a barrier, syncthreads.
Between blocks, there is no synchronisation: blocks run in any order, on any SM.
That rule is what lets CUDA scale. A small GPU runs a few blocks at a time, a big one runs many, and the same program works on both.
Stage 5: which element does a thread own? i equals blockIdx times blockDim, plus threadIdx.
Block 3, thread 5, with 256 threads per block: 3 times 256 plus 5, element 773.
If n is 1000, we need the ceiling of 1000 over 256: 4 blocks, 1024 threads. The last 24 threads find i not less than n, and do nothing. That is why the if is there.
n plus 255, over 256, in integer division, is exactly that ceiling.
Stage 6: images are two-dimensional, so blocks and grids can be too. Here, blocks of 16 by 16 threads, and a grid that covers the image.
Each thread computes a column x from the x parts of its indices, and a row y from the y parts.
Then, if the pixel is inside the image, it brightens it. Pixel x, y is at y times W plus x.
A 640 by 480 image with 16 by 16 blocks: a grid of 40 by 30, 1200 blocks.
Pixel 100, 50 belongs to block 6, 3, and is thread 4, 2 within it, because 100 is 6 times 16 plus 4, and 50 is 3 times 16 plus 2.

say.en: Stage 7: CUDA looks very different from vector code, but it is the same idea. A CUDA thread is the work of one element: one lane's share.
A thread block is like the body of a strip-mined vector loop: one strip of elements.
The grid is the whole loop.
And the if i less than n does the job of the vector length register: the hardware masks off the threads past the end.
The difference: the programmer writes code for one element, and the hardware groups threads into vector-like bundles. How it does that is the next video.

say.en: Now an exam question.

DAXPY with 5000 elements and 128 threads per block: how many blocks, and how many idle threads? The element of block 7, thread 100. The block and thread for element 4321. And a full HD image with 16 by 16 blocks. Pause and work it out.
a: the ceiling of 5000 over 128 is 40 blocks: 5120 threads, so 120 do nothing.
b: 7 times 128 plus 100: element 996.
c: divide 4321 by 128: 33, remainder 97. Block 33, thread 97.
d: 1920 over 16 is 120; 1080 over 16 is 67.5, rounded up to 68. 8160 blocks. Pixel 500, 300: 500 is 31 sixteens and 4, 300 is 18 sixteens and 12. Block 31, 18, thread 4, 12.
The usual slip: rounding down the number of blocks. 1080 over 16 rounded down leaves the bottom rows of the image unprocessed.
Let us walk the stages again.
The host CPU launches kernels on the device GPU. A kernel is written for one element; the loop becomes thousands of threads.
Threads form blocks, blocks form a grid. A thread finds its element from blockIdx, blockDim and threadIdx, in one or two dimensions. In vector terms: element, strip, loop.
Next video: how the hardware actually runs those threads. Warps, SIMT, and the streaming multiprocessor.
